_README: Values from the ORIGINAL paper: 'When Does TF-IDF Suffice? A Joint Study of
Accuracy, Adversarial Robustness, and Inference Latency for Toxicity
Detection in Multiplayer Game Chat' (Bhaumik & Berlin M. A., EDIGE 2026
Script 11 reads this file to build the old-vs-new columns and the flip
check in results/SUMMARY.md. Anything null is reported as 'not recorded'.
NOTE: two of the paper's Section IV methodology descriptions are
inconsistent with its own reported numbers. See _methodology_discrepancies
below. The values transcribed here are the paper's RESULTS, which are
self-consistent; the prose describing how they were obtained is not.

label_collapse_rule.paper_says: Sec IV-A: 'any utterance whose token-level annotation contains a non-O (non-background) tag is mapped to toxic'
label_collapse_rule.verdict: The paper's stated collapse rule is token-level and contradicts its own counts. The code must have used the utterance-level rule. Section IV-A needs correcting.

split_protocol.paper_says: Sec IV-B: 'approximately 59,820 utterances ... partition it 70/15/15 into train (41,874), validation (8,973), and test (8,973)'
split_protocol.verdict: A 41,874-row train split is impossible: CONDA_train.csv has 26,921 rows, and the entire corpus is 44,869 rows, not 59,820. However the paper's test split (8,973 rows, 6,628/2,345) matches CONDA_valid.csv exactly, so the actual protocol was almost certainly CONDA_train.csv -> 80/20 -> train/val with CONDA_valid.csv as test (train 21,531 / val 5,383), which is what the surviving memory note records and what this rebuild implements. Section IV-B needs correcting.
split_protocol.also_note: CONDA_test.csv is unlabelled (no intentClass), so it cannot have contributed to any scored split.

distilbert_latency_iterations.paper_says: Sec III-G: 'DistilBERT uses 100 timed predictions due to its higher per-example cost'
distilbert_latency_iterations.this_rebuild: 1000 timed predictions for every model including DistilBERT
distilbert_latency_iterations.verdict: Not an error, but the old DistilBERT latency figures rest on 10x fewer samples than the others, so their tail percentiles (p95/p99) are far less stable.

fig4_axis.paper_says: Fig 4 caption: 'Note the log-scale-friendly spread on the x-axis'
fig4_axis.observed: the plotted x-axis is linear (0-80 ms, evenly spaced)

splits._source: test counts from paper Sec IV-B; train/val from the surviving memory note, since the paper's stated 41,874/8,973 is arithmetically impossible

label_mapping._source: inferred: the unique mapping reproducing the paper's 2345/6628

metrics._source: paper Table I, plus Sec V-C for recall and false-positive counts

hyperparameters._note: The paper does not report the selected values, only the search protocol.

adversarial_macro_f1_drop._source: paper Table III (absolute drop, reported as negative; stored here as positive magnitudes to match this rebuild's abs_drop convention)

latency_ms._source: paper Table IV, CPU, mean single-example
latency_ms._caveat: DistilBERT timed with only 100 iterations in the original; 1000 here. The paper does not state whether timings are end-to-end or model-only, nor the RF n_jobs setting.

cascade._source: paper Sec VI-B (prose only; no table)
cascade._claim: 'under 15% of utterances need the transformer pass, cutting average cost by an order of magnitude while keeping most of DistilBERT's advantage on hard cases'

environment._note: This rebuild uses newer libraries (sklearn 1.9.x, torch 2.6.x); version differences are recorded in results/env.json.

conclusions._source: paper abstract, Sec V and Sec VI
_claims_in_prose: DistilBERT highest macro-F1 0.913, beating LR by 2.4 absolute points (p < 1e-14)
DistilBERT ~180x slower than LR on CPU (82.0 ms vs 0.45 ms)
classical classifiers lose up to 29 absolute points; DistilBERT at most 18
all six pairwise McNemar comparisons significant at alpha = 0.01
LR and NB saturate a 50 ms budget at over 40,000 messages/s per core
the toxic-class weight on 'report'/'commend' is an annotation artifact
